@@138479996 <h> The value of our institutions <p> Marcia LangtonPauline Hanson 's populist and mostly false declarations have changed little in 30 years . They are her personal grievances writ large for an audience hungry to attribute their own grievances to particular races and religions . <p> Pauline Hanson 's speech to the National Press Club should have convinced most people of her incapacity to govern our nation . She was on song with her written speech , cataloguing resentments and grievances , and was both unscripted and unhinged in response to media questioning -- which , to be fair , was n't all that incisive . <p> The media missed many opportunities to extract details of her so-called policies and electoral intentions . Voters are looking for answers , and they are entitled to be informed . Specifically , she said very little about what she believed was worth cherishing and protecting in Australia today . Surely it 's not politics , or politicians , but our institutions . <p> Institutions should matter more to us . Hanson 's Trumpian plan is to undermine or destroy all that is attractive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of our society . <p> I have always been impressed by the wisdom of 19th-century English economist and essayist Walter Bagehot , who observed that " the characteristic danger of great nations ... is that they may at last fall from not comprehending the great institutions which they have created " . <p> To my mind , Australia is defined by its institutions and practices . There is so much here to be protected . In some cases , these structures need further development and reform , but they should not be attacked . <p> Looking at the big picture , we have a strong Constitution that has defined our federation , governments and substantive political structures and processes . Importantly , we have compulsory voting . <p> Our economic institutions are very strong , with the Treasury , Finance and Industry departments , the Productivity Commission and an independent Reserve Bank . We are emerging as a global leader in the essential energy transition , with our concentration on renewables and storage . <p> We have a strong and professional public service -- in policy advice , design and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ targets . She clearly supports cuts , both in aggregate numbers and by closing departments against which she harbours prejudice . She has already singled out the Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water -- she joins United States President Donald Trump in claiming climate change is a hoax -- and the National Indigenous Affairs Agency . <p> Hanson started her National Press Club speech by refusing to acknowledge Country and First Australians and outlining her intention to cut assistance to First Nations communities . Her refusal to recognise Indigenous heritage as the basis on which modern Australia has been built is disturbing , as is her failure to respect the world 's longest-surviving culture of more than 60,000 years . <p> The undercurrent to most of Hanson 's remarks is a pining for a " white Australia " , despite a half-century of policy explicitly geared to developing a multicultural Australia , backed by strong anti-discrimination legislation , a Human Rights Commission and a culturally diverse broadcaster in SBS . <p> Institutions should matter more to us . Pauline Hanson 's Trumpian plan is to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this country , attacking the very fabric of our society . <p> Hanson made it clear she would abolish the AHRC . Similarly , she committed to fire the Sex Discrimination Commissioner , and she punched down hard on the two leaders . The AHRC has long been a target of certain members of the Coalition who do n't understand or accept the need to avoid division and hate speech and to treat all people with dignity and respect . It can not be denied that the AHRC has played a very important role in our society in enforcing anti-discrimination and hate speech laws against those , like Hanson , who seek to use inflammatory and racist rhetoric for some perceived short-term political gain . <p> I recall that former prime minister Tony Abbott , now Liberal Party president , rejected the AHRC report on the inhumane treatment of children in immigration detention . The conservative think tank the Institute for Public Affairs , at the time headed by Tim Wilson , wanted the commission abolished -- Abbott later appointed Wilson to lead it as " freedom commissioner " , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Discrimination Act . <p> It is very difficult to understand , let alone to accept , Hanson 's political thinking on immigration . The One Nation leader obviously believes she has a winning strategy with her proposed cuts to intake -- which the Coalition has also made a centrepiece of its agenda . Indeed , it has become a bit of a contest between them as to who can be the toughest on immigration , clearly to our national detriment and disgrace . <p> Hanson and the Coalition are calling it wrong . Recent polling from RedBridge Group on what primarily motivates One Nation voters suggests it 's not immigration but rather a desire to disrupt the two-party system and " politics as usual " . <p> And though they are all influenced by the experiences in Europe and the US , where surging migration has become a serious issue , these scenarios are not replicated in Australia . We are an immigrant nation . More than half our population is born overseas or has at least one parent born overseas . One of our major policy successes since World @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , multiracial , multireligious society that is the envy of many other countries -- and the benefit to Australians is a richness of experiences , opportunities and lifestyle . This needs to be recognised and seen as a work in progress to be nurtured , not undone by silly calls for a monoculture . <p> First-generation migrants will have significant sway in the outer metro and city seats that Hanson hopes to win -- and many of them will not be receptive to her message , including her anti-Muslim rhetoric . Moreover , though her remarks on immigration may be " raw meat " to her base , she ca n't push too hard -- business owners and farmers in regional communities in particular need the workforce . <p> One of Hanson 's most Trumpian approaches is her vilification of the media . To keep yourself and loved ones safe , it 's important to know your heat risk . <p> Anna GragertSenior Editor , Health and Home <p> Anna Gragert ( she/her/hers ) was previously the lifestyle editor at HelloGiggles , the deputy editor at So Yummy and the senior lifestyle editor at Hunker . Over the past 12 years , Anna has also written for the LA Times , Elle , Bust Magazine , Dazed , Apartment Therapy , Well+Good and more . At CNET , she 's a senior editor on the Healthy Home team , and her coverage includes health , wellness tech , meal kits and home and kitchen tech with a focus on the technology that aims to help us live our healthiest , happiest lives . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Weather Service tool can help you monitor your risk . <p> theburtons/Getty Images <p> The US National Weather Service is expecting a " significant , dangerous " heat wave across the Central and Eastern US from June 29 through July 3 , right before Fourth of July weekend . This is n't something to ignore , as extreme heat can cause heat stroke , heat exhaustion and other heat-related illnesses that could lead to medical complications and even death without emergency treatment . <p> So you can prepare yourself ahead of the heat wave , and during the entire summer , the National Weather Service has developed its NWS HeatRisk online tool to provide guidance on impactful heat across a seven-day forecast . Those who work in the heat or are sensitive to it , such as older adults , children and people on certain medications , should especially take heed . <h> How to find your heat risk <p> Under the seven-day forecast on the NWS HeatRisk tool 's main page , there 's a search bar where you can enter your address , ZIP code or city . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into it . <p> There will also be a pop-up showing the color-coded daily potential heat risk , the NWS weather forecast and the low and high temperatures for each day . <p> When you click on " Understanding HeatRisk " above the map , you can see the recommended actions for each category . For instance , if you 're dealing with extreme heat , you should stay hydrated and in a cool place , strongly consider canceling any outdoor activities , use air conditioning or find access to it and check on your neighbors or anyone you know who is more susceptible to heat-related illness . <p> What the HeatRisk map looks like for my location , Los Angeles , on Tuesday , June 30 . <p> NWS/Screenshot by CNET <h> What the heat risk tool shows <p> The NWS HeatRisk tool shows an entire map of the US , along with a key of five colors that correspond to the category for the risk of heat-related impacts : <p> Light green : Little to no risk <p> Yellow : Minor risk , which primarily affects people extremely @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Orange : Moderate risk , affecting those who are sensitive to heat , especially people without cooling or hydration , along with some health systems and industries . <p> Red : Major risk , affecting anyone without cooling or hydration , as well as health systems and industries . <p> Magenta , a dark purple : Extreme risk for rare and/or long-duration extreme heat with no overnight relief affecting anyone without cooling or hydration , as well as health systems , industries and infrastructure . <p> The NWS HeatRisk map for the entire US on Thursday , July 2 . <p> NWS/Screenshot by CNET <p> The key also shows the estimated population affected in each category . <p> You can select the forecast for today and up to six days in advance . At the top of the map , you can see when it was last updated . <h> The bottom line <p> Because of climate change , the risk of heat waves and extreme temperatures has increased , making it even more important to be prepared for these events that can harm our health . This handy NWS @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , so you can prepare and ensure that you , your loved ones and neighbors have enough water and a cool place to be once temperatures rise . <p> The information contained in this article is for educational and informational purposes only and is not intended as health or medical advice . @@138527559 <p> Here 's a trivia question for you : What branch on the tree of life has at least 14 million unique living members and can be found on every continent ? According to research out today , the answer is the tiny but mighty insect . <p> An international team of researchers conducted an exhaustive genetic survey of insects in Costa Rica to come up with the figure . At minimum , they estimate , there are likely somewhere between 14 and 20 million insect species in the world . These numbers are well above most current estimates and suggest scientists need to do a much better job at cataloging the vast diversity of insects that roam the Earth , the researchers say . <p> " Our study provides a baseline to understand how much more we need to learn about insects . We need this baseline to understand the scope of current insect declines , " study author Laura Melissa Guzman , an associate professor in the department of entomology at Cornell University , told Gizmodo . <h> The insect census <p> As you might imagine , it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ distinct species of insect there are in the world . It 's not exactly like you can get every bug to line up for a count , and many species in the same broad insect group can look remarkably similar to each other on a surface level . <p> Scientists have certainly tried , though , with the most recent estimates hovering around 6 million or so . Some studies have calculated these estimates by tallying up the known number of species from a specific group of insects in a region , then trying to gauge how many unknown species are likely to live in that same region . From that known to unknown ratio , scientists can ( hopefully ) extrapolate a rough sketch of total global insect species . <p> Guzman credits the origin of this research to senior author Mike Sharkey , a taxonomist who describes insects for a living . Though other studies have used beetles -- widely considered the most diverse group of insects in the world -- as the baseline insect to extrapolate from , Sharkey 's experience with parasitic wasps in Costa Rica @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ group to use as a proxy for all insectkind . <p> The team had access to a rich source of insect life : more than 1.5 million specimens collected over the years from 15 Malaise traps ( tent-like traps used for gathering wasps and other flying insects ) in the ? rea de Conservaci ? n Guanacaste ( ACG ) , a network of protected regions in the country with three major ecosystems : dry , cloud , and rain forests . Advances in genetics additionally allowed the team to rapidly identify distinct DNA sequences corresponding to a unique species within these specimens , a technique known as DNA barcoding -- a much improved method than trying to suss out a species by its physical features alone . Within these traps , they identified over 50,000 insect species . <p> The researchers then focused specifically on a highly diverse subfamily of wasps called Microgastrinae . They used a statistical method , borrowed from co-author Anne Chao , to calculate the ratio of known to unknown wasps in the ACG from three sources of specimens , the 15 main traps , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1,500 species of caterpillars , their insect hosts . From there , they estimated the total number of insect species in the ACG , nearly 333,000 . And finally , using four other groups of life as a reference ( trees , frogs , birds , and a specific family of moths ) , they arrived at their range for the global census : 14 to 20 million species . <h> A hidden world of bugs in need <p> The team 's findings , published Monday in the journal PNAS , are ultimately an educated guess . But Guzman says they took great care to double-check their math . <p> " Our estimate is a lower bound . We took a lot of effort at every step to evaluate our assumptions to understand whether we could be over or underestimating this lower bound , " she said . And if their numbers are right , then scientists are " dramatically underestimating the scope of what needs to be described , monitored , and protected , " she adds . <p> The researchers say there 's a lot more to go @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Guzman notes that scientists can use this kind of long-term trapping data to study how their numbers have changed as of late . The ACG database in particular covers decades , a rare thing for tropical insects . <p> " That gives us a window into whether populations are growing , shrinking , or shifting in response to climate change and land use , " she said . " Getting a better count of how many species exist is the first step . Understanding what is happening to those species over time is the next one . " <p> As much as insects might creep out plenty of people , there 's no denying they 're a remarkable success story of nature -- one that 's apparently even more impressive than we gave them credit for . 
@@138527562 <p> According to many true-believers , the biggest promise of AI is its potential to accelerate scientific discovery ; once-in-a-generation breakthroughs could one day become routine , thanks to algorithms . But some of the latest and most advanced models have taken that process to a new level by largely replacing human software engineers and revising much of the code it runs on . @@138527591 <p> El Ni ? o has arrived , which means we 're probably about to see some shifts in North American weather patterns . While the effects of El Ni ? o are most significant in the winter , all that extra heat emanating from the Pacific Ocean can influence summer weather , too . <p> The stronger the El Ni ? o , the more likely it is to produce wild weather , and this one looks like it 's going to be a doozy . According to the latest update from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration ( NOAA ) , there is a 63% chance that this El Ni ? o will become " very strong " by November . It 's still developing but strengthening rapidly , with sea surface temperatures jumping from 1.26 degrees Fahrenheit ( 0.7 degrees Celsius ) above average in early June to 1.98 degrees F ( 1.1 degrees C ) above average by mid-June . <p> So what does this mean for summer weather in the United States ? The short answer is : It 's complicated . El Ni ? @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ outcomes are n't guaranteed , even during a particularly strong El Ni ? o . With that said , experts pointed to certain trends each region of the U.S. may be more likely to experience this summer , from heightened risk of storms to more severe heat waves . <h> How El Ni ? o shifts North American weather patterns <p> El Ni ? o is the warm phase of the El Ni ? o-Southern Oscillation ( ENSO ) , a naturally recurring climate phenomenon in the equatorial Pacific Ocean . ENSO is the biggest driver of year-to-year climate variability on Earth . <p> During El Ni ? o , sea surface temperatures rise above average . As the trade winds weaken and warm Pacific water sloshes to the east , increased heat and moisture rise into the atmosphere and alter weather patterns around the globe . Strong El Ni ? os are more likely to shift the Pacific jet stream , which plays a key role in governing temperature and precipitation patterns across the United States . <p> When the jet stream moves south of its ENSO-neutral position , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ colder , wetter conditions . In the northern half of the country , the weather shifts toward warmer , drier conditions . <p> These impacts are much more prevalent in winter than in summer , Emily Becker , a research associate professor at the University of Miami 's Rosenstiel School of Marine , Atmospheric , and Earth Science , told Gizmodo . " El Ni ? o and La Ni ? a -- either phase -- are in the developing stages in the summer , so they peak in early winter , " she explained . " For that reason , and also because North American weather is governed by different processes in the summer versus the winter , we generally do n't really see very distinct impacts regionally the way we do during the winter . " <p> With that said , a few regions could still see some potential impacts from El Ni ? o in the upcoming months . Let 's break those down . <h> What the U.S. can expect during an El Ni ? o summer <p> The biggest impact El Ni ? o has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Becker said . As a result , states along the East and Gulf coasts can expect fewer named storms this year , and those that do develop will likely be weaker . NOAA 's seasonal outlook reflects that pattern , calling for below-normal activity in the Atlantic Basin , with just eight to 14 named storms , three to six hurricanes , and one to three major hurricanes . <p> The Pacific hurricane season will be a different story . During El Ni ? o , warmer sea surface temperatures pump more energy into the atmosphere , helping storms form and intensify . This phase of ENSO is also associated with reduced vertical wind shear , the change in wind speed and direction between altitudes of roughly 5,000 and 35,000 feet ( 1,500 and 10,700 meters ) . Wind shear can literally rip storms apart , so reducing this condition also aids formation and intensification . For these reasons , El Ni ? o can amplify Pacific hurricane season , Becker said . <p> Unsurprisingly , NOAA anticipates above-normal activity in the eastern and central Pacific this summer , with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and five to nine major hurricanes . California and the Pacific Northwest will therefore be at greater risk of extreme storms this summer . <p> In terms of more moderate impacts , El Ni ? o could increase precipitation in the Southwest , though we likely wo n't see a significant change until late summer or early fall , Dan Collins , a meteorologist at NOAA 's Climate Prediction Center , told Gizmodo in an email . " The stronger impacts can be seen for the Midwest and Great Lakes in the summer , and an El Ni ? o can increase the chances of cooler than average temperatures , and less than average rainfall , " Collins said . <p> As El Ni ? o tilts the odds toward warmer-than-average temperatures in the northern U.S. , forecasters will be on the lookout for heatwaves . " Early-season heat is a major hazard because communities are n't yet acclimatized ; even non-extreme temperature increases can cause health issues for at-risk individuals , " Amanda Reinhart , a meteorologist at NOAA 's Weather Prediction Center , told Gizmodo in an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is shaping up to be particularly strong , that does n't mean severe weather anomalies are guaranteed this summer . " The impacts are n't necessarily more severe with a stronger El Ni ? o , they 're just more predictable , " Becker explained . " The stronger the El Ni ? o , the more likely that we will see these expected impacts . " <p> It 's important to note that climate change is already exacerbating extreme weather across the U.S. , making it increasingly difficult to distinguish the impacts of natural climate variability from those of long-term warming trends . @@138527850 <p> While crops in dry air conditions tend to close the stomata , or the pores on their leaves , to prevent water loss , this process has also been understood to limit carbon dioxide intake and reduce plant growth . <p> But the new research has found the leaves were able to compensate by increasing their " mesophyll conductance " , allowing carbon dioxide to enter the photosynthetic machinery more easily and maintain CO2 concentrations in a conserved range that supports the efficient use of carbon and nitrogen resources . <p> " Even though the first gate closes a bit , the second gate will open , " lead researcher Dr Xingyu Hu said . <p> " We did n't expect the plants to coordinate all sorts of different parts to make them better cope with climate change and allow better use of resources . " <p> Dr Hu said a better understanding of the process would play a big role in guiding more efficient water management and irrigation , as well as supporting agronomic modelling more widely . <p> " When should we irrigate the plant ? " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the plant ? " <p> " For the future , if we consider the modelling of crop species , how they will respond to the heat and dryness of the future climate change conditions , we should take both the stomatal part and mesophyll part into account . <p> " We also need to better think about the coordination among all these different components . " <p> A plant 's capacity to self-regulate in this way could be an important factor to consider and isolate when analysing crop performance , but it could also be a beneficial trait to breed towards . <p> Dr Hilary Stuart-Williams said it was possible that agricultural selection had already played a part in augmenting the mechanism in modern crops . <p> " Crops are being bred for productivity , which means without knowing what 's going on inside them , selecting for various factors which make them grow better , " Dr Stuart-Williams said . <p> " So it 's quite likely that gm mesophyll conductance is one of the factors that has coincidentally been improved . <p> " Plants have a very @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deal of opportunity for improvement in there . " <p> While the study only examined cotton , sunflower and dwarf bean plants , the researchers expected the mechanism could be shared by other crops using the C3 photosynthetic pathway , such as wheat , barley , oats , rice and most plant species , but not necessarily in the same way in C4 crops such as sorghum , sugarcane and maize . <p> Dr Hu said the research was only in its infancy , and the team had now started looking beyond crops at tropical tree species .

That February , the U.S. Office of Personnel Management abruptly fired 880 NOAA employees . Two months later , NOAA approved over 1,000 deferred resignations or buyouts . These sweeping staff cuts forced the National Weather Service ( NWS ) , the forecasting arm of NOAA , to halt or reduce weather balloon launches at 11 locations . <p> " We 're going to lose data because of this staffing , " Michael Morgan , an atmospheric scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and former NOAA administrator , said at the time . " And that loss of data then translates into less precise forecasts , more uncertainties in the forecast . " <p> Before @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ day ( once in the morning and once in the evening ) from 100 locations . " I 'm not able to predict severe weather with the confidence I normally would . That is extremely concerning . " <h> Deflated data <p> Weather balloons , also known as sounding balloons or radiosondes , carry instruments that measure temperature , wind , humidity , and pressure high into the atmosphere . Meteorologists feed the data they gather into forecast models , providing a snapshot of current conditions so that the models can predict future conditions . <p> Federal forecasters have relied on weather balloons for more than a century , though today 's models are far more advanced . This technology has stood the test of time because @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a vertical snapshot of the atmosphere in real time . Unlike satellites , weather balloons gather direct measurements and therefore play a crucial role in ensuring forecast accuracy . <p> According to Cappucci , the NWS has historically launched balloons around 7 a.m. and 7 p.m . ET daily , but that 's no longer happening . Following the Trump administration 's staffing cuts , many sites that have n't stopped weather balloon operations altogether have pushed morning launches to early afternoon . <p> " That 's not helpful for morning severe weather forecasts , " he explains . " In other words , you get less lead time . Less advanced notice . Quicker ramp-ups and ramp-downs to the forecast . We 're not able to get jet stream , temperature , moisture or wind profiles of the atmosphere each morning like we otherwise would . " <p> Dealing with the logistical challenges of unreliable daily forecasts is a nuisance , but when it comes to predicting severe weather , a lack of data can be dangerous . In May , the start of peak tornado season for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ three-quarters of scheduled morning weather balloon launches . <p> " That 's unacceptable , " U.S. Representative Sharice Davids ( D-Kan. ) said at the time . " Kansans deserve confidence that the systems meant to keep them safe are fully operational during tornado season and meteorologists deserve the reliable data they need to do their jobs . " <p> With climate change exacerbating the threat of extreme weather , it 's never been more important to ensure that federal forecasters have access to accurate , real-time atmospheric measurements . @@138585652 <h> Scientists celebrate the rare visit of southern right whales to Sydney <p> The sudden appearance of a pair of rare southern right whales in the middle of a shipping lane in Port Botany and in the shadow of the nation 's busiest airport sparked both excitement and an emergency response from experts and authorities , who swung into action to protect them from a gauntlet of modern threats . <p> A rare southern right whale and its calf have visited Port Botany and Bondi in the midst of the annual whale migration . <p> The world has not always been so kind to southern right whales , so named because they were the " right " species to hunt back in the whaling days . <p> Southern rights typically swim at less than 10 kilometres an hour , slower than other targeted species . When harpooned they floated rather than sank . They provided more oil than other species and their bones were fine and flexible , perfect for the fabrication of everyday items like umbrella ribs and riding crops . <p> By the time commercial whaling was abandoned @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ estimated there were between 1500 and 5000 humpbacks left , but as few as 300 southern rights . Only the blue whale suffered a greater population decline . Worse , while humpbacks calf every two to three years , southern rights do so only every three to four years . The interval stretches when conditions are poor . The humpback population has made an extraordinary comeback , but southern rights have not . <p> Advertisement <p> All this helps explain the excitement with which Dr Vanessa Pirotta greeted the arrival of the mother and calf in Botany Bay on Monday afternoon . <p> " We do n't see them often , this species ... we do n't expect to see huge numbers of them , so when we see them , we know that it 's a big deal , figuratively and literally , " she said . <p> Even better , they appeared to be in good health after a season feeding on krill in the southern oceans . <p> So rare are the animals that the survival of this mother and calf alone could have an impact on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at Macquarie University who specialises in the study of whales . " If we lose a productive female of a very fragmented population that could have population-level impact , " she says . <p> Advertisement <p> Botany Bay , also known by its Indigenous name Gamay , is much cleaner than a few decades ago , with the restoration of oysters and sea grass , and reduced pollution . <p> Yet threats remain . On Monday afternoon , Pirotta held her breath as the mother unwittingly guided her calf into a shipping lane and then sank beneath the surface as a cargo ship approached . <p> " I was holding my breath , she held her breath , and she was just obviously sitting there . And then after the ship passed , she rose up . It was almost like she was waiting for it , " she said . <p> The mother and calf were watched over by NPWS staff as they navigated a busy waterway . <p> The pair could not have known that the humans who once hunted their kind were now watching over them . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ranger group based in La Perouse -- kept a weather eye on the pair to protect them from collision in the busy waterway . <p> Advertisement <p> Shipping strikes are one of the key threats to the estimated 10,000 to 15,000 southern rights that now survive , but not the only one . Climate change is shrinking Antarctic ice coverage , which in turn is reducing the amount of krill upon which the whales feed . <h> Related Article <p> The krill population is also falling because it is being harvested for use as dog food and fish oil supplements . Whales are at risk of entanglement in so-called ghost nets abandoned by deep-sea trawlers , and when they swim up the Australian coast they must navigate the threat of shark nets . <p> By Tuesday morning , the pair had moved on to Bondi Beach . Pirotta expects the mother may spend some time off the NSW coast , which marks the northern end of the animal 's annual migration , suckling her calf in the warm shallow waters , before returning to the deep south .
